promptBlocks.label: Prompt 4
promptBlocks.text:
NANO BANANA PRO · THE SET
Image 1 is the location: the hotel entrance with the cream stone facade, the coffered canopy with warm downlights and hanging brass lanterns, the glass entrance doors, the wet pavement, and the blue-hour city skyline. Keep this architecture and mood, but remove the black car, the luggage carts, and the staff standing at the doors. The curb in front is empty.
Images 2 to 5 are character reference sheets. From each one, take only the person's face, hair, and outfit. Ignore the grid layout, the grey background, and every label.
Image 5 is the security guard: black button-up shirt, black trousers, a clear coiled earpiece, and a small black penlight.
Image 2 is the young woman with black bangs and a septum ring, in the oversized white "Racing '90" tee over sheer black lace sleeves, the black satin slip skirt, the red bead necklace, and the red patent shoulder bag.
Image 3 is the young man with the round wire glasses, the black leather jacket, the white shirt, and the red tie.
Image 4 is the curly-haired bearded man with tattoo sleeves, the cream graphic tee, the teal cap, the washed wide-leg jeans, and the tan suede boots.
Scene: blue hour. A queue of people waits along the facade beneath the canopy, held in a lane by polished brass stanchions with black velvet ropes. At the very front of the queue, set flush into the stone pavement, is a round brushed-steel hatch about one and a half metres wide, with a thin polished steel rim and a faint seam across its centre. It is a trapdoor, closed for now.
The woman from Image 2 stands on the hatch. The security guard from Image 5 stands just in front of her, seen from behind over his right shoulder at a slight diagonal: we see the back of his head, his ear with the earpiece, part of his jaw in profile, and his raised right arm aiming the switched-on penlight straight into her face. She squints and leans back slightly in the hard white beam.
Next in line, waiting a step behind the rope, is the young man from Image 3, watching with a neutral face. Behind him stands the bearded man from Image 4. Behind them the queue continues deep into the frame along the building: thirty or more ordinary strangers in dark coats and casual night-out clothes, of varied ages, chatting and checking phones, softly out of focus.
Camera: a real photograph taken on an iPhone, held just behind the guard's shoulder at chest height, vertical frame. The image carries the texture of an ARRI Alexa with ARRI Signature Prime lenses: gentle low-contrast rendering, soft highlight roll-off, lifted blacks, creamy falloff into the background, with the queue receding diagonally toward the vanishing point.
Light: warm amber glow from the canopy downlights and lanterns, cool blue ambient from the sky, and the penlight's small hard cool-white beam as the brightest point, on her face. Wet pavement with soft reflections of the lanterns and the steel rim of the hatch.
Realism: unretouched skin with natural pores, real fabric wrinkles, slight phone sensor noise in the shadows, a muted desaturated grade. No car, no captions, no signage lettering, no watermark, and nothing copied from the character sheet labels.

promptBlocks.label: Prompt 5
promptBlocks.text:
NANO BANANA PRO · EDIT · THE SWAP
Edit Image 1. Keep everything in Image 1 exactly the same: the camera angle, framing, location, canopy and lanterns, the wet pavement, the brass stanchions and velvet ropes, the steel hatch, the guard with the penlight, the woman on the hatch, the young man with the glasses and red tie, every stranger in the long queue, the lighting, the low-contrast grade, and the grain.
Change only one person: the third person in the queue, the man in the teal cap and cream graphic tee standing directly behind the young man with the red tie. Replace him completely with the man from Image 2, a character reference sheet. From Image 2 take only his face, his short dense curly dark brown hair, his moustache and goatee with stubble, and his outfit: the glossy crinkled burgundy leather bomber jacket worn open, the white button-up shirt, the cream straight-leg jeans, and the burgundy suede running sneakers. He wears the black square sunglasses from Image 2. Ignore the grid, the labels, and the studio background of Image 2.
He stands in exactly the same spot, at the same scale and height, in the same relaxed standing pose, waiting in line behind the young man and partly overlapped by him in the same way, head turned slightly toward the hatch. He is lit by the same warm amber canopy light and cool blue ambient as everyone around him, with matching softness, grain, and color, so he sits naturally in the photograph. The glossy leather picks up small warm highlights from the lanterns.
No cap, no tattoos, no other changes anywhere in the image.

promptBlocks.label: Prompt 7

tutorialHtml:
DENIZ AKKABAK · ULTIMATE REALISM TUTORIAL · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

MADE IN ARCADS · arcads.ai

Ultimate Cinematic Realism Blueprint

Cast from Pinterest, lock four characters into studio charts, build the set, design the hero prop and direct a 30-second door-check film with native dialogue — every step made in Arcads.

A TUTORIAL BY DENIZ AKKABAK · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

PIPELINE GPT IMAGE 2.5 → NANO BANANA PRO → SEEDANCE 2.5 FORMAT 4:3 · 30 S · 1080P PLATFORM ARCADS

Every viral door check runs on one question: are you a real person? This film turns that question on the viewer. A bouncer shines a penlight into each face, a steel trapdoor swallows anyone who fails, and the joke only lands if the audience genuinely cannot tell who is synthetic. That makes realism the punchline — not a nice-to-have. This blueprint walks through the entire build exactly as we made it in Arcads: casting outfits from Pinterest, locking four characters into studio-grade charts, compositing the set, designing the hero book and directing a single 30-second Seedance 2.5 generation with four distinct voices. Every prompt is printed verbatim, and every “why it works” is tied to the exact line that does the work.

THE PIPELINE AT A GLANCE

  1. 01

    Cast from Pinterest

    Pair one face with one outfit per character. The face never borrows the outfit’s body, and the outfit never borrows the face.

  2. 02

    Lock the charts

    GPT Image 2.5 turns each pair into a five-angle studio sheet with labelled detail tiles — the continuity bible every later model restores from.

  3. 03

    Build the set

    Nano Banana Pro drops the cast into the real location; a surgical edit then swaps me into the queue without moving a single pixel of the rest.

  4. 04

    Design the prop

    GPT Image 2.5 renders the hero book in four angles with the title, cover portraits and Arcads logo intact.

  5. 05

    Shoot the film

    Seedance 2.5 reads six references and directs fourteen shots, four voices and a working trapdoor in one 30-second generation.

THE MODEL MAP — WHICH MODEL FOR WHICH JOB

  1. 01

    GPT Image 2.5

    Charts, typography and anything with text. It obeys reference scopes literally and spells labels, prints and logos cleanly. We ran 16:9 for charts and 9:16 for the book, 2K, quality high.

  2. 02

    Nano Banana Pro

    Location compositing and keep-everything-change-one-thing edits. The richest material texture at 4K, with the aspect ratio matched to the frame you need.

  3. 03

    Nano Banana 2.1

    The fast draft lane. Useful for blocking a composition cheaply, but in our side-by-side test its faces drifted toward the outfit references — never trust it with final identity.

  4. 04

    Seedance 2.5

    The director. Reference to Video mode, up to 30 seconds, multi-shot editing, native dialogue and sound. We rendered 30 s, 4:3, 1080p, audio on, MOV, high bitrate.

STEP 01 — PINTEREST → ARCADS

Casting From Pinterest

Realism starts before the first prompt. For each character we pulled two images: a face, which owns identity, and a Pinterest outfit, which owns wardrobe. Keeping them in separate images is the whole trick — a model can only blend what you hand it inside one picture, so the face reference decides bone structure, skin and hair, while the outfit reference decides cut, fabric and print and its model’s face is explicitly banned. The guard needed no outfit photo at all: plain black workwear is easier to write than to find. For the third character I skipped casting entirely and used my own chart.

REFERENCE INPUTS — ONE FACE, ONE OUTFIT

STEP 02 — GPT IMAGE 2.5

Locking the Cast — Character Charts

Before committing, we generated the same chart side by side with Nano Banana 2.1, Nano Banana Pro and GPT Image 2.5. GPT Image 2.5 won clearly: the closest identity, the cleanest labels and the fewest leaks. Nano Banana Pro pulled a stranger’s eyes into a detail tile, and Nano Banana 2.1 drifted the faces toward the outfit models. Every chart uses the same three-slot architecture — WARDROBE ONLY, IDENTITY ONLY, LAYOUT ONLY — each with a NEVER clause that names what it must not contribute. The layout slot is simply any finished chart: it teaches the grid, the grey seamless and the label typography without lending a face.

Chart 1 — the woman

REFERENCE INPUTS — ATTACH IN THIS ORDER

Image 1 — the Pinterest outfit. Image 2 — the face. Image 3 — a finished chart as the layout template (we used my own).

OUTPUT

Chart 2 — the young man, and the crop trick

Our first male charts kept inheriting the outfit model’s face: the model reads a person in a photo as a package, so the jaw and moustache rode along with the jacket. The fix happens before the prompt. Crop the outfit photo below the chin, and cut a second, tight crop for the one accessory that sits on the face. The outfit model’s face never enters the generation, so it cannot leak. Note how the prompt then tells the model what to ignore inside the crops — hands, drinks, phones, papers.

REFERENCE INPUTS — ATTACH IN THIS ORDER

Image 1 — the face. Image 2 — outfit, neck down. Image 3 — accessory band only. Image 4 — the woman’s chart as layout.

OUTPUT

Chart 3 — the guard

No outfit photo here. When the wardrobe is generic, writing it is more precise than finding it: matte twill, a sharp trouser crease, a dull steel buckle, a clear coiled earpiece, a machined penlight. The prompt also gives him his job — checking faces with a small flashlight — so two panels rehearse the exact gesture the film needs.

REFERENCE INPUTS — ATTACH IN THIS ORDER

Image 1 — the face. Image 2 — the woman’s chart as layout.

OUTPUT

STEP 03 — NANO BANANA PRO

Building the Set

The set is a real hotel entrance photo plus the four charts. Two decisions matter. First, the location is told what to lose — the car, the luggage carts, the doormen — so the frame belongs to the queue. Second, the trapdoor is written as an engineered object with a size, a polished rim and a centre seam, because the film will open it later and the model needs to know where it splits. The camera lines carry the realism anchors that run through the whole project: a real photograph taken on an iPhone, with the texture of ARRI Signature Prime glass and a deliberately low-contrast grade.

REFERENCE INPUTS — ATTACH IN THIS ORDER

OUTPUT

The swap — putting myself in line

Nano Banana Pro is the strongest model we have for “keep everything, change one thing”. The prompt first lists everything that must survive — angle, lanterns, stanchions, hatch, every stranger, the grain — and only then names the single change, down to the spot, the scale, the overlap with the person in front and the light that must fall on the new leather. The sunglasses are on deliberately: the film opens with me hidden behind them.

REFERENCE INPUTS — ATTACH IN THIS ORDER

OUTPUT

STEP 04 — GPT IMAGE 2.5

Designing the Hero Prop

The ending pays off on an object, so the object has to be worth the close-up. We designed the book with the cast on its cover and rendered it from four angles on white, so the video model has every face of the prop — front, spine, back and page edges. GPT Image 2.5 is the right engine because the cover is mostly typography: four stacked lines in a condensed display face, small caps, frame numbers and a logo that must not be redrawn. The material language — soft-touch linen, white foil, spot-UV portraits, a crimson ribbon — is what makes it read as a real object rather than a mockup.

REFERENCE INPUTS — ATTACH IN THIS ORDER

Image 1 — the Arcads logo. Images 2–5 — the character charts, used for faces only.

OUTPUT

STEP 05 — SEEDANCE 2.5

Directing the Film

One generation, thirty seconds, fourteen shots. Seedance 2.5 in Reference to Video mode reads six images and treats each one exactly as scoped: the set for blocking and grade, four charts for restoring faces, the book for the final hold. The woman starts one step behind the hatch rather than on it, so the film opens with movement instead of a frozen still. Each beat is a timecode, a physical camera position and an end state; every line of dialogue appears once, inside braces, with its own voice described in the VOICES block. Everything here runs in the same Arcads studio — start in Arcads and attach the references in the order below.

REFERENCE INPUTS — ATTACH IN THIS ORDER

SETTINGS

Seedance 2.5 — Reference to Video · 30 s · 4:3 · 1080p · native audio on · MOV · high bitrate

OUTPUT — FOUR CHECKPOINTS

STEP 06

Anatomy — Why It Reads as Real

  1. 01

    The contract

    “30-second cinematic multi-shot sequence … Hard cuts between shots, real-time action, no slow motion.” The first line tells Seedance it is cutting an edit, not drifting through one shot, and “real-time” removes the floaty slow-motion that gives AI footage away.

  2. 02

    Hybrid realism

    “filmed on an iPhone, with the texture of an ARRI Alexa and ARRI Signature Prime lenses: low contrast, lifted blacks …” The phone supplies believability — handheld micro-shake, sensor grain, “no smooth gimbal” — while the cinema glass supplies falloff. Low contrast reads as footage, not a render.

  3. 03

    Scoped references

    “LOCATION, BLOCKING AND GRADE ONLY … Not a first frame … Ignore the grid, labels and studio background.” Every slot states what it controls and what it must not. Without this, the model opens on the still or prints chart labels into the street.

  4. 04

    Restore, don’t describe

    “Use every character sheet to restore each face precisely.” The charts are the source of truth; the short text descriptions are a second lock. Upstream, the crop trick guarantees there is nothing foreign in a face to restore.

  5. 05

    Angles that prove the set

    “Camera inside the dark shaft looking straight up through the open round hatch …” Fake sets only work from the front. A top-down drop and a POV from inside the pit show the space from angles a viewer has never seen — the strongest evidence that the place exists.

  6. 06

    Physiological truth

    “the pupil visibly constricts in a quick smooth reflex … slowly widens back.” Real pupils tighten under light and relax after it. Getting the biology right in an extreme macro is the moment the audience stops doubting.

  7. 07

    Sound, voices, insurance

    “<heavy steel latch clunk and hydraulic hiss> … Each line is spoken once … extra spoken words, narration of the prompt, garbled book title” Timecoded SFX give every cut a physical cause, the VOICES block keeps four speakers distinct, and the negative prompt blocks the classic failures before they happen.

THE RESULT

Output — the Door Check

Audit it against the prompt: the woman steps onto the steel before the beam hits her, the shaft POV catches the next in line peering down, my sunglasses come off the moment my foot lands and never return, the pupil tightens and relaxes, and the final hold reads the cover cleanly. If the title ever wobbles, planar-track the GPT Image 2.5 book render over the hold.

THE BOUNCER ASKS THE QUESTION YOUR AUDIENCE IS ALREADY ASKING

If the bouncer can’t tell, neither can the feed.

Swap the hotel for a club, the penlight for a scanner, the trapdoor for a sliding wall — the skeleton carries any test-and-reveal format. Cast from real references, lock every face into a chart, build the set as a still, design the prop that pays off the ending, then let one long reference-to-video generation direct the edit. Realism isn’t a filter you add at the end; it is a chain of small, scoped decisions, and every link in this blueprint is one of them.

Every model in this blueprint — GPT Image 2.5, Nano Banana Pro and Seedance 2.5 — lives in one studio. Cast your own characters, build your set and direct your first 30-second film in Arcads.
